datasets.title: Airline flights
datasets.description: Thirty-two flights between ten airports, each in its own time zone, from 8 to 11 March 2025 (US clocks moved forward on 9 March), plus passengers and their bookings. All times are stored as `timestamptz`; the session time zone is UTC.
datasets.setup:
CREATE TABLE airports (code char(3) PRIMARY KEY, city text NOT NULL, country char(2) NOT NULL, tz text NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE flights (
  id int PRIMARY KEY, flight_no text NOT NULL, tail text NOT NULL,
  origin char(3) NOT NULL REFERENCES airports(code), dest char(3) NOT NULL REFERENCES airports(code),
  dep_at timestamptz NOT NULL, arr_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
  status text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('scheduled','arrived','cancelled')), seats int NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE passengers (id int PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL, country char(2) NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE bookings (
  id int GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  flight_id int NOT NULL REFERENCES flights(id), passenger_id int NOT NULL REFERENCES passengers(id),
  class text NOT NULL CHECK (class IN ('economy','business')), fare numeric(8,2) NOT NULL, seat text,
  status text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'confirmed' CHECK (status IN ('confirmed','cancelled')), booked_at timestamptz NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE seat_requests (passenger_id int NOT NULL, flight_id int NOT NULL, seat text NOT NULL, fare numeric(8,2) NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE refunds (booking_id int PRIMARY KEY, passenger_id int NOT NULL, amount numeric(8,2) NOT NULL);

datasets.title: Sensor readings
datasets.description: Five sensors on one site that should report every 10 minutes from 1 March 2025 00:00 to 4 March 11:50 UTC: about 1,900 readings with an outage, short gaps, a sensor that went silent, one that never reported, NULL values and a few duplicated rows.
datasets.setup:
CREATE TABLE sensors (id int PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL UNIQUE, kind text NOT NULL, tz text NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE readings (sensor_id int NOT NULL REFERENCES sensors(id), ts timestamptz NOT NULL, value numeric(5,2));
INSERT INTO sensors VALUES
 (1,'greenhouse-a','temperature','Europe/Berlin'),(2,'greenhouse-b','temperature','Europe/Berlin'),
 (3,'cellar','temperature','Europe/Berlin'),(4,'attic','humidity','Europe/Berlin'),(5,'garage','temperature','Europe/Berlin');
-- n = 1, 2, 3 … numbers the 10-minute slots; m = minutes since the start. Values follow a daily curve plus a fixed wobble.
INSERT INTO readings (sensor_id, ts, value)
SELECT s, ts,
  CASE
    WHEN s = 1 AND (n % 97 = 0 OR n = 75) THEN NULL
    WHEN s = 1 THEN 22 + 5 * sin(2 * pi() * (m - 360) / 1440) + ((n * 37) % 7 - 3) / 10.0
    WHEN s = 2 THEN 20 + 3 * sin(2 * pi() * (m - 420) / 1440) + ((n * 13) % 5 - 2) / 10.0
    WHEN s = 3 THEN 12 + 0.6 * sin(2 * pi() * (m - 600) / 1440) + ((n * 11) % 3 - 1) / 10.0
    ELSE 60 + 12 * cos(2 * pi() * (m - 240) / 1440) + ((n * 7) % 9 - 4) / 10.0
  END
FROM generate_series(1, 4) AS s,
     generate_series(timestamptz '2025-03-01 00:00+00', timestamptz '2025-03-04 11:50+00', interval '10 minutes') WITH ORDINALITY AS g(ts, n),
     LATERAL (SELECT (n - 1) * 10 AS m) AS mm
WHERE NOT (s = 2 AND ts >= '2025-03-02 03:00+00' AND ts < '2025-03-02 06:00+00')
  AND NOT (s = 3 AND (ts = '2025-03-01 20:10+00' OR ts BETWEEN '2025-03-03 12:00+00' AND '2025-03-03 12:30+00'))
  AND NOT (s = 4 AND ts >= '2025-03-03 18:00+00')
ORDER BY ts, s;
-- a flaky uplink delivered three messages twice
INSERT INTO readings SELECT * FROM readings
WHERE sensor_id = 2 AND ts IN ('2025-03-01 08:00+00', '2025-03-01 08:10+00', '2025-03-02 12:00+00');
CREATE INDEX ON readings (sensor_id, ts);

datasets.title: Lending library
datasets.description: A small library: books and their authors (many-to-many, including a co-written book and an anonymous one), members, and loans from June 2024 to the end of June 2025. "Today" in these exercises is 2025-06-30.
datasets.setup:
CREATE TABLE authors (id int PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL, born int);
CREATE TABLE books (id int PRIMARY KEY, title text NOT NULL, isbn text UNIQUE, published int NOT NULL, pages int, copies int NOT NULL CHECK (copies >= 0));
CREATE TABLE book_authors (book_id int REFERENCES books(id), author_id int REFERENCES authors(id), PRIMARY KEY (book_id, author_id));
CREATE TABLE members (id int GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL, email text NOT NULL UNIQUE, joined date NOT NULL, tier text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'standard' CHECK (tier IN ('standard','gold')));
CREATE TABLE loans (
  id int GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  book_id int NOT NULL REFERENCES books(id), member_id int NOT NULL REFERENCES members(id),
  loaned_on date NOT NULL, due_on date NOT NULL, returned_on date);
CREATE TABLE fines (loan_id int PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES loans(id), amount numeric(6,2) NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE member_import (import_id int PRIMARY KEY, email text NOT NULL, name text NOT NULL, tier text NOT NULL);

exercises.title: Departures from Heathrow
exercises.task: Return `flight_no`, `dest` and `dep_at` of every flight with origin `LHR`, earliest departure first.
exercises.solution: SELECT flight_no, dest, dep_at FROM flights WHERE origin = 'LHR' ORDER BY dep_at;
exercises.explanation: `dep_at` is a `timestamptz`, an absolute instant, so sorting by it is a true chronological order no matter which zone each airport is in.

exercises.title: Flights by status
exercises.task: Return `status` and `flights` (the number of flights with that status).
exercises.solution: SELECT status, count(*) AS flights FROM flights GROUP BY status;
exercises.explanation: `GROUP BY status` makes one group per distinct value and `count(*)` counts the rows in each.

exercises.title: Confirmed bookings without a seat
exercises.task: Return the `id`, `flight_id` and `passenger_id` of every **confirmed** booking that has no seat assigned.
exercises.solution: SELECT id, flight_id, passenger_id FROM bookings WHERE seat IS NULL AND status = 'confirmed';
exercises.explanation: A missing seat is NULL, which only `IS NULL` matches. Several cancelled bookings also lack a seat, so forgetting the status filter returns too many rows.

exercises.title: How long are flights out of JFK?
exercises.task: For flights with origin `JFK`, return `flight_no`, `dep_at` and `duration` = arrival minus departure (an `interval`).
exercises.solution: SELECT flight_no, dep_at, arr_at - dep_at AS duration FROM flights WHERE origin = 'JFK';
exercises.explanation: Subtracting two `timestamptz` values gives the real elapsed time as an `interval`, regardless of the time zones of the two airports; converting both to local wall-clock times first would be off by the zone difference.

exercises.title: Fare statistics
exercises.task: Over **confirmed** bookings only, return one row: `cheapest`, `dearest`, and `average` (rounded to 2 decimals) of `fare`.
exercises.solution:
SELECT min(fare) AS cheapest, max(fare) AS dearest, round(avg(fare), 2) AS average
FROM bookings WHERE status = 'confirmed';
exercises.explanation: Without `GROUP BY`, aggregates collapse the whole filtered table into a single row. The cancelled bookings would pull the average down if they were not filtered out.

exercises.title: Hired in 2022
exercises.task: Return the `name` and `hired_on` of everyone hired during calendar year 2022 (1 January to 31 December inclusive), sorted by `hired_on`.
exercises.hint: A half-open range `>= start AND < next start` never misses the last day.
exercises.explanation: Two people were hired exactly on the boundaries (1 January and 31 December), so `> '2022-01-01'` or `< '2022-12-31'` each lose one row. The half-open form `>= start AND < next_start` is the habit to build: it also works unchanged for `timestamp` columns, where `BETWEEN … AND '2022-12-31'` would stop at midnight.

exercises.title: Total compensation in Sales
exercises.task: For every employee in department 2 (Sales), return `name` and `total_comp` = `salary * (1 + commission_pct)`, treating a missing commission as 0.
exercises.hint: Any arithmetic with NULL gives NULL.
exercises.solution:
SELECT name, salary * (1 + COALESCE(commission_pct, 0)) AS total_comp
FROM employees WHERE dept_id = 2;
exercises.explanation: Kwame has no commission, so `salary * (1 + commission_pct)` is NULL for him rather than his salary. `COALESCE(commission_pct, 0)` substitutes the zero the task asks for.

exercises.title: Headcount per department id
exercises.task: Return `dept_id` and `headcount` (number of employees) for every `dept_id` value that appears in `employees`, **including** the group of employees with no department (`dept_id` NULL).
exercises.solution: SELECT dept_id, count(*) AS headcount FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id;
exercises.explanation: `GROUP BY` puts all NULLs in one group, so the two people without a department show up as a row with `dept_id` NULL. Departments with nobody in them do not appear at all, because grouping only sees rows that exist in `employees`.

exercises.title: Five best-paid employees
exercises.task: Return `name` and `salary` of the five highest-paid employees, highest first.
exercises.solution: SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 5;
exercises.explanation: `ORDER BY … DESC LIMIT n` is the standard top-N. The fifth and sixth salaries differ here, so the result is well defined; when they tie, add a tie-breaker column or use `FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS WITH TIES`.

exercises.title: No manager or no department
exercises.task: Return the `name` of every employee who has no manager **or** no department (or both).
exercises.solution: SELECT name FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL OR dept_id IS NULL;
exercises.explanation: The CEO has neither, the contractor has only a manager. `IS NULL` is the only test that matches a missing value; `dept_id = NULL` is never true.

exercises.title: Rows versus values
exercises.task: For each sensor that has readings, return `sensor_id`, `readings` (number of rows) and `with_value` (number of rows whose `value` is not NULL).
exercises.hint: `count(*)` and `count(column)` are not the same thing.
exercises.solution: SELECT sensor_id, count(*) AS readings, count(value) AS with_value FROM readings GROUP BY sensor_id;
exercises.explanation: `count(*)` counts rows; `count(value)` counts only non-NULL values. Every aggregate except `count(*)` skips NULLs, which is why greenhouse-a’s average is not dragged down by its missing readings.

exercises.title: Lowest and highest value per sensor
exercises.task: Return `sensor_id`, `min_value` and `max_value` for every sensor that has readings.
exercises.solution: SELECT sensor_id, min(value) AS min_value, max(value) AS max_value FROM readings GROUP BY sensor_id;
exercises.explanation: `min` and `max` ignore NULLs, so a sensor with gaps still gets real numbers. The garage sensor has no rows, so it forms no group.

exercises.title: Readings in a 12-hour window
exercises.task: Return one column `n`: the number of readings from sensor 3 with `ts` from 2025-03-03 06:00 UTC (inclusive) up to 18:00 UTC (exclusive).
exercises.solution:
SELECT count(*) AS n FROM readings
WHERE sensor_id = 3 AND ts >= '2025-03-03 06:00+00' AND ts < '2025-03-03 18:00+00';
exercises.explanation: A half-open interval `>= start AND < end` counts each 10-minute slot once; `BETWEEN` includes both ends and would also count the 18:00 reading. Writing the offset (`+00`) in the literal pins the instant regardless of the session time zone.

exercises.title: The five most recent readings
exercises.task: Return `ts` and `value` of the five most recent readings of sensor 2, newest first.
exercises.solution: SELECT ts, value FROM readings WHERE sensor_id = 2 ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 5;
exercises.explanation: `ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 5` walks the `(sensor_id, ts)` index backwards and stops after five rows, so it stays fast however large the table grows.

exercises.title: When did greenhouse-a fail to measure?
exercises.task: Return the `ts` of every sensor-1 reading whose `value` is NULL, in time order.
exercises.solution: SELECT ts FROM readings WHERE sensor_id = 1 AND value IS NULL ORDER BY ts;
exercises.explanation: A row that exists with a NULL value is different from a missing row: here the sensor reported, but without a measurement. `IS NULL` finds the first kind; finding the second needs a gap analysis.

exercises.title: Books currently out
exercises.task: Return `id`, `book_id` and `member_id` of every loan that has not been returned yet.
exercises.solution: SELECT id, book_id, member_id FROM loans WHERE returned_on IS NULL;
exercises.explanation: A loan that is still out has no return date: NULL. `returned_on = NULL` matches nothing, because a comparison with NULL is never true.

exercises.title: Classics first
exercises.task: Return `title` and `published` of books published before 1980, ordered by `published`, and by `title` among books from the same year.
exercises.solution: SELECT title, published FROM books WHERE published < 1980 ORDER BY published, title;
exercises.explanation: Two books came out in 1968 and two in 1979, so ordering by year alone leaves their relative order undefined; the second sort key settles it.

exercises.title: How long are the books?
exercises.task: Return one row: `books` (number of books), `with_pages` (books whose page count is known) and `avg_pages` (average of the known page counts, rounded to 1 decimal).
exercises.solution: SELECT count(*) AS books, count(pages) AS with_pages, round(avg(pages), 1) AS avg_pages FROM books;
exercises.explanation: `count(pages)` and `avg(pages)` skip NULLs, so the average is over the 13 known values. `sum(pages) / count(*)` would treat unknown books as zero pages and use integer division on top.

exercises.title: Label unknown page counts
exercises.task: Return `title` and `pages_label`: the page count as text, or the word `unknown` when it is missing.
exercises.hint: `COALESCE` needs all its arguments to have one type.
exercises.solution: SELECT title, COALESCE(pages::text, 'unknown') AS pages_label FROM books;
exercises.explanation: `COALESCE(pages, 'unknown')` fails, because the result must have a single type and `'unknown'` is not an integer. Cast the number to text first.

exercises.title: How many people borrowed in 2025?
exercises.task: Return one column `borrowers`: the number of **different** members with at least one loan dated in 2025.
exercises.solution:
SELECT count(DISTINCT member_id) AS borrowers FROM loans
WHERE loaned_on >= '2025-01-01' AND loaned_on < '2026-01-01';
exercises.explanation: `count(*)` counts loans, not people; `count(DISTINCT member_id)` counts each member once.

exercises.title: Customers in the US
exercises.task: Return the `name` and `email` of every customer whose `country` is `US`, sorted by `name`.
exercises.hint: Filter with `WHERE`, sort with `ORDER BY`.
exercises.solution: SELECT name, email FROM customers WHERE country = 'US' ORDER BY name;
exercises.explanation: String literals use single quotes. Without `ORDER BY` PostgreSQL returns rows in whatever order is cheapest, which is not guaranteed to be stable.

exercises.title: Customers without an email
exercises.task: Return the `id` and `name` of customers who have **no** email address.
exercises.hint: `= NULL` never matches anything.
exercises.solution: SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE email IS NULL;
exercises.explanation: Comparing anything with NULL using `=` gives NULL, not true, so `WHERE email = NULL` returns no rows. Use `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`.

exercises.title: Products in a price range
exercises.task: Return `name` and `price` of products priced from 59.00 to 999.00, **both ends included**, most expensive first.
exercises.solution: SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price BETWEEN 59 AND 999 ORDER BY price DESC;
exercises.explanation: `BETWEEN a AND b` is inclusive at both ends, the same as `>= a AND <= b`. Two products sit exactly on the boundaries, so `> 59 AND < 999` loses them.

exercises.title: Orders per status
exercises.task: Return `status` and `orders` (how many orders have that status).
exercises.solution: SELECT status, count(*) AS orders FROM orders GROUP BY status;
exercises.explanation: `GROUP BY` forms one group per distinct status, and `count(*)` counts the rows in each.

exercises.title: Case-insensitive name search
exercises.task: Return the `name` of every customer whose name contains the letters `li`, in **any** letter case.
exercises.hint: `LIKE` is case-sensitive.
exercises.solution: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE name ILIKE '%li%';
exercises.explanation: Both matches start a word with a capital, so `LIKE '%li%'` finds nothing. `ILIKE` compares case-insensitively; `lower(name) LIKE '%li%'` works too, and a leading `%` means no ordinary B-tree index can help either way.

exercises.title: Three most expensive products
exercises.task: Return `name` and `price` of the three most expensive products, most expensive first.
exercises.solution: SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 3;
exercises.explanation: `LIMIT` applies after `ORDER BY`, so you get the top three by price. Without the `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT 3` returns three arbitrary rows.

exercises.title: Routes by city name
exercises.task: Return `id`, `flight_no`, `from_city` and `to_city` for every flight.
exercises.hint: You need the `airports` table twice.
exercises.solution:
SELECT f.id, f.flight_no, o.city AS from_city, d.city AS to_city
FROM flights f
JOIN airports o ON o.code = f.origin
JOIN airports d ON d.code = f.dest;
exercises.explanation: Each foreign key needs its own join, so the same table appears twice under different aliases. Joining once on `code IN (origin, dest)` produces two rows per flight instead.

exercises.title: Departure time on the airport clock
exercises.task: Return `id`, `flight_no` and `local_dep`: the departure as a `timestamp` (without time zone) on the wall clock of the **origin** airport.
exercises.hint: `timestamptz AT TIME ZONE 'zone'` gives a plain `timestamp` in that zone.
exercises.solution:
SELECT f.id, f.flight_no, f.dep_at AT TIME ZONE a.tz AS local_dep
FROM flights f JOIN airports a ON a.code = f.origin;
exercises.explanation: Applied to a `timestamptz`, `AT TIME ZONE` converts the instant to local wall-clock time in that zone and drops the zone, taking daylight saving into account (AA100 leaves New York at 18:00 both before and after 9 March, which is 23:00 and then 22:00 UTC). Casting to `timestamp` instead would use the session zone, UTC.

exercises.title: Departures on 10 March, local time
exercises.task: Return `id` and `flight_no` of every flight that departs on **10 March 2025 in the local time of its origin airport**.
exercises.explanation: The departure date depends on whose calendar you use: AI111 leaves Delhi at 00:10 on 11 March local time, which is still 10 March in UTC, and UA837 leaves San Francisco on the evening of 10 March, already 11 March in UTC. Filtering on `dep_at::date` uses the session zone and gets both wrong.

exercises.title: How full is each flight?
exercises.task: For every flight that is not cancelled, return `id`, `flight_no`, `booked` (number of **confirmed** bookings, 0 if none), `seats`, and `load_pct` = booked / seats × 100 rounded to 1 decimal.
exercises.hint: `count(*)` counts the NULL row an outer join makes for an empty flight.
exercises.solution:
SELECT f.id, f.flight_no, count(b.id) AS booked, f.seats,
       round(100.0 * count(b.id) / f.seats, 1) AS load_pct
FROM flights f
LEFT JOIN bookings b ON b.flight_id = f.id AND b.status = 'confirmed'
WHERE f.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY f.id;
exercises.explanation: Three traps: an inner join drops AA100 on 9 March, which has no bookings; with a `LEFT JOIN`, `count(*)` reports 1 for it, while `count(b.id)` counts only real matches; and the booking-status filter must sit in the `ON` clause, because in `WHERE` it would discard the NULL row again. `GROUP BY f.id` allows selecting other `flights` columns because `id` is the primary key.

exercises.title: Passengers with nothing booked
exercises.task: Return the `name` of every passenger who has **no confirmed booking** (they may have none at all, or only cancelled ones).
exercises.solution:
SELECT p.name FROM passengers p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM bookings b WHERE b.passenger_id = p.id AND b.status = 'confirmed');
exercises.explanation: Liam has bookings, but all of them are cancelled. `LEFT JOIN bookings … WHERE b.id IS NULL AND b.status = 'confirmed'` (or with the status test anywhere in `WHERE`) cannot find him; the status condition has to be part of the join condition or of the `NOT EXISTS` subquery.

exercises.title: Who reports to whom
exercises.task: Return `employee` (name) and `manager` (the manager’s name) for **every** employee. The CEO has no manager: show NULL.
exercises.hint: Join `employees` to itself under a second alias.
exercises.explanation: A self-join uses two aliases for the same table. It must be a `LEFT JOIN`: an inner join drops the CEO, whose `manager_id` is NULL and matches nobody.

exercises.title: Well-paid departments
exercises.task: Return `department` (name) and `avg_salary` (rounded to 2 decimals) for departments whose average salary is **above 124000**.
exercises.solution:
SELECT d.name AS department, round(avg(e.salary), 2) AS avg_salary
FROM departments d JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.name
HAVING avg(e.salary) > 124000;
exercises.explanation: `WHERE` filters rows before grouping; a condition on an aggregate belongs in `HAVING`, which filters groups. Engineering clears the bar by a few hundred, Finance does not; a `WHERE salary > 124000` would instead average only the high earners and let every department through.

exercises.title: Earning more than the boss
exercises.task: Return `employee`, `salary`, `manager`, `manager_salary` for every employee whose salary is strictly greater than their manager’s.
exercises.explanation: Join each employee row to its manager row, then compare columns across the two aliases. An inner join is right here: people without a manager have nobody to out-earn.

exercises.title: Departments with nobody in them
exercises.task: Return the `name` of every department that has no employees.
exercises.hint: Try `NOT IN (SELECT dept_id FROM employees)` first, and see what happens.
exercises.solution:
SELECT d.name FROM departments d
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id = d.id);
exercises.explanation: The classic trap: `NOT IN (SELECT dept_id FROM employees)` returns **no rows**, because the list contains NULLs and `x NOT IN (…, NULL)` is NULL, never true. `NOT EXISTS` (or `LEFT JOIN … WHERE e.id IS NULL`) is NULL-safe and usually planned as an efficient anti-join.

exercises.title: Completed years of service
exercises.task: Return `name` and `years` = the number of **completed** years between `hired_on` and `2025-12-31` (an int; someone hired 2022-12-31 has completed exactly 3).
exercises.hint: `age(later, earlier)` returns a calendar interval.
exercises.solution: SELECT name, extract(year FROM age(date '2025-12-31', hired_on))::int AS years FROM employees;
exercises.explanation: `age()` counts calendar years and months, so anniversaries land exactly. Dividing the day difference by 365 drifts by a day every leap year: Ben, hired 2022-01-01, is 1460 days in, which `/ 365` calls 4 years although his fourth anniversary is the next day.

exercises.title: Hourly averages
exercises.task: For sensor 1 on 1 March 2025 (UTC), return `hour` (the start of each hour, a `timestamptz`) and `avg_value` rounded to 2 decimals, in time order.
exercises.solution:
SELECT date_trunc('hour', ts) AS hour, round(avg(value), 2) AS avg_value
FROM readings
WHERE sensor_id = 1 AND ts >= '2025-03-01 00:00+00' AND ts < '2025-03-02 00:00+00'
GROUP BY hour ORDER BY hour;
exercises.explanation: `date_trunc('hour', ts)` maps every reading to the start of its hour, so grouping by it buckets the data. On a `timestamptz` it truncates in the session time zone (UTC here). `avg` skips the NULL readings rather than counting them as zero.

exercises.title: Six-hour buckets reveal an outage
exercises.task: For sensor 2 on 2 March 2025 (UTC), return `bucket` (start of each 6-hour bucket: 00:00, 06:00, 12:00, 18:00 UTC) and `readings` (rows in it), in time order.
exercises.hint: `date_trunc` only knows whole units; `date_bin` takes any stride.
exercises.solution:
SELECT date_bin('6 hours', ts, timestamptz '2025-03-01 00:00+00') AS bucket, count(*) AS readings
FROM readings
WHERE sensor_id = 2 AND ts >= '2025-03-02 00:00+00' AND ts < '2025-03-03 00:00+00'
GROUP BY bucket ORDER BY bucket;
exercises.explanation: `date_bin(stride, ts, origin)` snaps each timestamp to the start of its bucket counted from `origin`. A full bucket holds 36 readings; the first one is short because of the three-hour outage, and the duplicated noon message makes another one long.

exercises.title: Daily figures on the site’s calendar
exercises.task: For sensor 1, group readings by **local calendar day** in the sensor’s time zone (`sensors.tz`). Return `day` (a `date`), `readings` (rows) and `avg_value` rounded to 2 decimals.
exercises.solution:
SELECT (r.ts AT TIME ZONE s.tz)::date AS day, count(*) AS readings, round(avg(r.value), 2) AS avg_value
FROM readings r JOIN sensors s ON s.id = r.sensor_id
WHERE r.sensor_id = 1
GROUP BY day;
exercises.explanation: Berlin is one hour ahead of UTC in March, so its day starts at 23:00 UTC the evening before. `ts::date` uses the session zone (UTC) and puts six readings per day on the wrong date; `ts AT TIME ZONE tz` gives local wall-clock time first.

exercises.title: Sensors that have gone quiet
exercises.task: Return the `name` of every sensor with **no** reading at or after 2025-03-04 00:00 UTC, including sensors that never reported at all.
exercises.solution:
SELECT s.name FROM sensors s
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM readings r WHERE r.sensor_id = s.id AND r.ts >= '2025-03-04 00:00+00');
exercises.explanation: Phrase it as "there is no recent reading" and the never-seen garage sensor qualifies naturally. Joining readings and testing `max(ts) < …` per sensor misses it, because a sensor with no rows has no group.

exercises.title: Cold, normal, hot, or missing
exercises.task: Classify every sensor-1 reading as `cold` (below 18), `normal` (18 to 25 inclusive), `hot` (above 25) or `missing` (NULL value). Return `class` and `readings` (count per class).
exercises.hint: What does a CASE with `ELSE 'hot'` do with NULL?
exercises.solution:
SELECT CASE WHEN value IS NULL THEN 'missing'
            WHEN value < 18 THEN 'cold'
            WHEN value <= 25 THEN 'normal'
            ELSE 'hot' END AS class,
       count(*) AS readings
FROM readings WHERE sensor_id = 1
GROUP BY class;
exercises.explanation: `CASE` takes the first branch whose condition is true. Every comparison with NULL is NULL, not false, so NULL values fall through to `ELSE`: without an explicit `IS NULL` branch they are counted as hot.

exercises.title: Books with their authors
exercises.task: Return one row per book: `title` and `authors`, the author names in alphabetical order joined with `', '`. A book with no known author gets NULL.
exercises.solution:
SELECT b.title, string_agg(a.name, ', ' ORDER BY a.name) AS authors
FROM books b
LEFT JOIN book_authors ba ON ba.book_id = b.id
LEFT JOIN authors a ON a.id = ba.author_id
GROUP BY b.id, b.title;
exercises.explanation: A many-to-many relationship goes through the link table. Both joins must be outer joins, or *Beowulf* disappears; `string_agg` ignores the NULL name and returns NULL for an empty group. The `ORDER BY` inside the aggregate fixes the order of names within the string.

exercises.title: Overdue today
exercises.task: As of 2025-06-30, return `member` (name), `title` and `days_overdue` (an integer) for every loan that is not returned and whose `due_on` is **before** 2025-06-30.
exercises.solution:
SELECT m.name AS member, b.title, date '2025-06-30' - l.due_on AS days_overdue
FROM loans l
JOIN members m ON m.id = l.member_id
JOIN books b ON b.id = l.book_id
WHERE l.returned_on IS NULL AND l.due_on < date '2025-06-30';
exercises.explanation: Subtracting two `date` values gives an integer number of days; subtracting timestamps would give an interval instead. One loan is due exactly on the 30th and is not overdue yet, so `<=` is wrong.

exercises.title: Books nobody has borrowed
exercises.task: Return the `title` of every book that has never been loaned.
exercises.solution:
SELECT b.title FROM books b
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM loans l WHERE l.book_id = b.id);
exercises.explanation: `NOT EXISTS` is the anti-join: keep rows with no match. `LEFT JOIN loans l … WHERE l.id IS NULL` is equivalent. `NOT IN` works here only because `loans.book_id` is `NOT NULL`; with a nullable column it would return nothing.

exercises.title: Authors with several books
exercises.task: Return `name` and `books` (number of books in the catalogue) for authors with **at least two** books. Co-written books count for each author.
exercises.solution:
SELECT a.name, count(*) AS books
FROM authors a JOIN book_authors ba ON ba.author_id = a.id
GROUP BY a.id, a.name
HAVING count(*) >= 2;
exercises.explanation: Counting through the link table credits *Good Omens* and *Nightfall* to both of their authors. Group by the id as well as the name, so two different authors who share a name are not merged.

exercises.title: Copies on the shelf
exercises.task: For every book return `title`, `copies`, `on_loan` (loans not yet returned) and `available` = copies − on_loan.
exercises.solution:
SELECT b.title, b.copies, count(l.id) AS on_loan, b.copies - count(l.id) AS available
FROM books b
LEFT JOIN loans l ON l.book_id = b.id AND l.returned_on IS NULL
GROUP BY b.id;
exercises.explanation: The open-loan condition must be in the `ON` clause: in `WHERE`, `l.returned_on IS NULL` is also true for the NULL row of a book with no loans at all, but false for a book whose loans are all returned, which then vanishes. `count(l.id)` gives 0 where `count(*)` would give 1.

exercises.title: Revenue per top-level category
exercises.task: For each **top-level** category (no parent), return `category` and `revenue` = the sum of `quantity * unit_price` over all non-cancelled orders of products in that category or its direct subcategories. Sort by revenue, highest first.
exercises.hint: Map each product to its top-level category with `COALESCE(parent_id, id)`.
exercises.solution:
SELECT top.name AS category, sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
FROM order_items oi
JOIN orders o     ON o.id = oi.order_id AND o.status <> 'cancelled'
JOIN products p   ON p.id = oi.product_id
JOIN categories c ON c.id = p.category_id
JOIN categories top ON top.id = COALESCE(c.parent_id, c.id)
GROUP BY top.name
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
exercises.explanation: `COALESCE(c.parent_id, c.id)` rolls a subcategory up to its parent in one step (enough for a two-level tree; deeper trees need a recursive CTE). Filtering cancelled orders in the `JOIN … ON` or in `WHERE` is equivalent here because it is an inner join.

exercises.title: Customers who never really bought
exercises.task: Return `id` and `name` of customers with **no order other than cancelled ones** (no orders at all also counts).
exercises.solution:
SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status <> 'cancelled');
exercises.explanation: Alan placed one order and cancelled it; Ken never ordered. A `LEFT JOIN orders … WHERE o.id IS NULL` finds only Ken, unless the status test moves into the `ON` clause. `NOT EXISTS` with the condition inside the subquery says exactly what is meant.

exercises.title: Orders per month
exercises.task: Return `month` (the first day of the month, as a `date`) and `orders` (number of orders placed that month, any status), oldest month first. Months without orders are not listed.
exercises.solution:
SELECT date_trunc('month', ordered_at)::date AS month, count(*) AS orders
FROM orders GROUP BY month ORDER BY month;
exercises.explanation: `date_trunc('month', …)` maps every timestamp to the start of its month, so grouping by it buckets the orders; the cast turns the result into a `date`. Grouping by `extract(month …)` alone would merge the same month of different years.

exercises.title: Orders over 1,000
exercises.task: Return `order_id` and `total` (sum of `quantity * unit_price`) for every **non-cancelled** order whose total is above 1000.
exercises.solution:
SELECT oi.order_id, sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS total
FROM order_items oi JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY oi.order_id
HAVING sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) > 1000;
exercises.explanation: The status test is about rows, so it goes in `WHERE`; the total exists only per group, so its test goes in `HAVING`. Testing `unit_price > 1000` in `WHERE` instead would keep only single expensive lines and miss orders that add up past the limit.

exercises.title: Products by price band
exercises.task: Put every product in a band: `budget` (under 100), `mid` (100 up to but not including 1000), `premium` (1000 or more). Return `band` and `products` (how many products are in it).
exercises.solution:
SELECT CASE WHEN price < 100 THEN 'budget'
            WHEN price < 1000 THEN 'mid'
            ELSE 'premium' END AS band,
       count(*) AS products
FROM products GROUP BY band;
exercises.explanation: `CASE` picks the first branch that is true, so each later test only needs the upper bound. `GROUP BY band` may refer to the output alias; repeating the whole `CASE` expression works too.

exercises.title: Average order value per country
exercises.task: For each customer country, return `country` and `avg_order`: the average **order** total (sum of its lines) over non-cancelled orders, rounded to 2 decimals. Countries without such orders are not listed.
exercises.hint: Compute one total per order first, then average those.
exercises.solution:
SELECT c.country, round(avg(t.total), 2) AS avg_order
FROM (
  SELECT order_id, sum(quantity * unit_price) AS total FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id
) t
JOIN orders o ON o.id = t.order_id AND o.status <> 'cancelled'
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.country;
exercises.explanation: Joining customers straight to `order_items` and taking `avg(quantity * unit_price)` averages **lines**, not orders, and an order with two lines counts twice. Aggregating to one row per order in a derived table first gives the right granularity.

exercises.title: Two-leg trips out of London
exercises.task: Find connections: a first flight from `LHR` and a second flight leaving the first one’s destination between **1 and 8 hours (inclusive)** after the first arrives. Neither flight may be cancelled and the second must not fly back to `LHR`. Return `first_leg`, `second_leg` (flight ids), `via` (airport code) and `layover` (interval).
exercises.solution:
SELECT a.id AS first_leg, b.id AS second_leg, a.dest AS via, b.dep_at - a.arr_at AS layover
FROM flights a
JOIN flights b ON b.origin = a.dest
              AND b.dep_at BETWEEN a.arr_at + interval '1 hour' AND a.arr_at + interval '8 hours'
WHERE a.origin = 'LHR' AND b.dest <> 'LHR'
  AND a.status <> 'cancelled' AND b.status <> 'cancelled';
exercises.explanation: A self-join pairs each flight with every candidate onward flight, and the time window belongs in the join condition. `BETWEEN` is inclusive at both ends, and one connection has a layover of exactly 8 hours. Without the status tests the cancelled Paris–New York and Singapore–Sydney flights would look like valid connections, and the flights from New York back to London are returns, not onward legs.

exercises.title: Aircraft turned around in under an hour
exercises.task: For each aircraft (`tail`), look at its non-cancelled flights in departure order. Return `tail`, `flight_id`, `next_flight_id` and `turnaround` (next departure minus this arrival) wherever the turnaround is **less than 1 hour**.
exercises.solution:
SELECT tail, flight_id, next_flight_id, turnaround FROM (
  SELECT tail, id AS flight_id,
         lead(id) OVER w AS next_flight_id,
         lead(dep_at) OVER w - arr_at AS turnaround
  FROM flights WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY tail ORDER BY dep_at)
) t
WHERE turnaround < interval '1 hour';
exercises.explanation: `lead()` looks one row ahead within the aircraft’s own partition, so each row can compare its arrival with the next departure. Cancelled flights must be removed *before* the window is computed (in `WHERE`), or the cancelled Paris shuttle shows up as a phantom turnaround. The last flight of each aircraft has no next row, so `turnaround` is NULL and the `<` test drops it. A named `WINDOW` avoids repeating the same definition.

exercises.title: Busiest local day at each airport
exercises.task: For each origin airport, find the **local** calendar date (airport time zone) with the most departures, counting all flights. Return `origin`, `day` (a `date`) and `departures`; when several days tie, return all of them.
exercises.explanation: Window functions run after `GROUP BY`, so `rank() OVER (… ORDER BY count(*) DESC)` ranks the grouped days directly, and `rank` gives every tied day the number 1. Grouping by the UTC date moves late-evening New York and just-after-midnight Delhi flights to another day and changes the winners; `DISTINCT ON` or `LIMIT 1` would drop ties.

exercises.title: Everywhere you can get from Delhi
exercises.task: Treat every non-cancelled flight as a route (ignore times). Return `code` and `legs` = the minimum number of flights needed to reach each airport from `DEL`. Do not list `DEL` itself; unreachable airports are not listed.
exercises.hint: The route graph has cycles. Carry the list of airports visited so far and refuse to revisit one.
exercises.explanation: Without the `seen` array the recursion loops forever (London to New York and back). The only route to Auckland is cancelled, so it must not appear. Tracking the path keeps each walk simple, and `min(legs)` picks the shortest of the several paths to each airport. PostgreSQL also offers a `CYCLE` clause that does this bookkeeping for you.

exercises.title: The full org chart
exercises.task: Return `name`, `depth` (CEO = 0, their direct reports = 1, …) and `path`, the chain of names from the CEO down to the employee joined with `' > '` (for the CEO just `Ruth Ortega`). One row per employee.
exercises.hint: `WITH RECURSIVE`: start from the row with no manager, then join children onto the rows found so far.
exercises.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE chart AS (
  SELECT id, name, 0 AS depth, name AS path FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, c.depth + 1, c.path || ' > ' || e.name
  FROM employees e JOIN chart c ON e.manager_id = c.id
)
SELECT name, depth, path FROM chart;
exercises.explanation: The non-recursive part seeds the CEO; each iteration joins the next level of reports onto the previous one until no new rows appear. Carrying `depth` and `path` along in the recursive part is how you build per-row context that a plain join cannot.

exercises.title: Everyone below each manager
exercises.task: For every employee who manages at least one person, return `manager` (name) and `reports` = the number of people below them at any depth (direct and indirect).
exercises.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE below AS (
  SELECT manager_id AS boss, id AS emp FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT b.boss, e.id FROM below b JOIN employees e ON e.manager_id = b.emp
)
SELECT m.name AS manager, count(*) AS reports
FROM below b JOIN employees m ON m.id = b.boss
GROUP BY m.name;
exercises.explanation: Generate every (ancestor, descendant) pair: start with direct pairs and extend each by one level per iteration. Counting direct reports only (`GROUP BY manager_id`) gives the CEO 4 instead of 19.

exercises.title: Three lowest salary levels per department
exercises.task: For each department (skip employees with no department), return `department`, `name`, `salary` for employees whose salary is among the **three lowest distinct salaries** in their department. Ties are all included.
exercises.hint: `dense_rank()` numbers distinct values without gaps.
exercises.explanation: Diego and Hana both earn 110000, the third-lowest Engineering salary, so the right answer has four Engineering rows. `row_number()` or a `LIMIT` per group silently drops one of them; `dense_rank()` gives tied values the same number.

exercises.title: Every raise, and how big it was
exercises.task: From `salary_history`, return one row per raise: `name`, `effective_from`, `old_salary`, `new_salary`, and `pct` = the increase in percent rounded to 1 decimal. An employee’s first history row is not a raise.
exercises.solution:
SELECT name, effective_from, old_salary, salary AS new_salary,
       round(100.0 * (salary - old_salary) / old_salary, 1) AS pct
FROM (
  SELECT e.name, h.effective_from, h.salary,
         lag(h.salary) OVER (PARTITION BY h.emp_id ORDER BY h.effective_from) AS old_salary
  FROM salary_history h JOIN employees e ON e.id = h.emp_id
) t
WHERE old_salary IS NOT NULL;
exercises.explanation: `lag()` reads the previous row in the window, here the previous salary of the same employee; partitioning keeps one person’s history from bleeding into the next. Window functions cannot appear in `WHERE`, so filter the first rows out in an outer query. Note `100.0 *`: with all-integer operands the division would truncate.

exercises.title: Salaries as of a date
exercises.task: Using `salary_history`, return `name` and `salary` = what each employee earned **on 2023-01-01** (the latest history row effective on or before that day). Leave out employees with no such row.
exercises.hint: `CROSS JOIN LATERAL (… ORDER BY effective_from DESC LIMIT 1)`.
exercises.solution:
SELECT e.name, h.salary
FROM employees e
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT salary FROM salary_history s
  WHERE s.emp_id = e.id AND s.effective_from <= '2023-01-01'
  ORDER BY s.effective_from DESC LIMIT 1
) h;
exercises.explanation: A `LATERAL` subquery runs per outer row and may reference it, so it can pick "the latest row before X" per employee. Two raises take effect exactly on 2023-01-01 (inclusive) and one on 2023-01-02 (excluded), so `<` versus `<=` matters. `CROSS JOIN` drops employees whose subquery returns nothing; `LEFT JOIN LATERAL … ON true` would keep them.

exercises.title: Find the gaps
exercises.task: For every sensor, find places where the next reading arrives **more than 10 minutes** after the previous one. Return `sensor_id`, `gap_from` (last reading before the gap), `gap_to` (first reading after) and `missing` = number of 10-minute slots skipped (an integer).
exercises.explanation: `lead(ts)` pairs every reading with the next one of the same sensor, which turns "find the gaps" into a simple filter on the difference. Duplicated rows produce a zero difference and are harmless here. A sensor that stopped for good (the attic) has no next row and so no gap: spotting that needs a comparison with "now".

exercises.title: Hot spells
exercises.task: For sensor 1, find every run of consecutive readings with `value > 25` (a NULL reading breaks a run). Return `run_start`, `run_end` (first and last `ts` of the run) and `readings` in the run.
exercises.hint: Number all readings, number the hot ones, and subtract: the difference is constant within a run.
exercises.solution:
SELECT min(ts) AS run_start, max(ts) AS run_end, count(*) AS readings
FROM (
  SELECT ts, value,
         row_number() OVER (ORDER BY ts)
       - row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY value > 25 ORDER BY ts) AS grp
  FROM readings WHERE sensor_id = 1
) t
WHERE value > 25
GROUP BY grp;
exercises.explanation: Within a run of hot readings both row numbers grow by one per row, so their difference stays constant and identifies the island; any reading in between bumps the overall number only. NULL values land in their own partition (`value > 25` is NULL), so they break a run like a cool reading does: the first day’s spell is split in two by a missing measurement.

exercises.title: Six-reading moving average
exercises.task: For sensor 1 between 2025-03-01 00:00 and 01:50 UTC inclusive, return `ts`, `value` and `moving_avg`: the average of this reading and the 5 before it (fewer at the start), rounded to 2 decimals. Order by `ts`.
exercises.solution:
SELECT ts, value,
       round(avg(value) OVER (ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN 5 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS moving_avg
FROM readings
WHERE sensor_id = 1 AND ts BETWEEN '2025-03-01 00:00+00' AND '2025-03-01 01:50+00'
ORDER BY ts;
exercises.explanation: With `ORDER BY` but no frame clause, a window aggregate defaults to `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, a running average over everything so far. `ROWS BETWEEN 5 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` slides a fixed six-row window instead.

exercises.title: Average over the last hour, not the last six rows
exercises.task: For sensor 2 readings from 2025-03-02 06:30 to 07:30 UTC inclusive, return `ts`, `value` and `avg_1h`: the average of **all** sensor-2 readings with timestamps in `[ts − 1 hour, ts]`, rounded to 2 decimals. Order by `ts`.
exercises.hint: Two traps: the frame unit, and where you filter.
exercises.solution:
SELECT ts, value, avg_1h FROM (
  SELECT ts, value,
         round(avg(value) OVER (ORDER BY ts RANGE BETWEEN interval '1 hour' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS avg_1h
  FROM readings WHERE sensor_id = 2
) t
WHERE ts BETWEEN '2025-03-02 06:30+00' AND '2025-03-02 07:30+00'
ORDER BY ts;
exercises.explanation: A `RANGE` frame with an interval offset is defined by time, so at 06:30, just after the 03:00–06:00 outage, it holds only the readings since 06:00; `ROWS 6 PRECEDING` would reach back to readings from before the outage. And because window functions run after `WHERE`, the window must be computed in a subquery over the whole series and filtered outside, or the frame could never see earlier rows.

exercises.title: Show the missing slots
exercises.task: For sensor 3, list every 10-minute slot from 2025-03-03 11:30 to 13:00 UTC inclusive: `slot` (timestamptz) and `value` (NULL where no reading exists). Order by `slot`.
exercises.solution:
SELECT g.slot, r.value
FROM generate_series(timestamptz '2025-03-03 11:30+00', timestamptz '2025-03-03 13:00+00', interval '10 minutes') AS g(slot)
LEFT JOIN readings r ON r.sensor_id = 3 AND r.ts = g.slot
ORDER BY g.slot;
exercises.explanation: You cannot select rows that do not exist, so generate the expected timeline and outer-join the data onto it. Putting `r.sensor_id = 3` in `WHERE` instead of `ON` would turn the outer join back into an inner one and drop the empty slots.

exercises.title: First and last value of each day
exercises.task: For every sensor and UTC day with readings, return `sensor_id`, `day` (a `date`), `first_value` (the value of the earliest reading that day) and `last_value` (the value of the latest).
exercises.hint: `last_value()` with the default frame is a famous trap.
exercises.solution:
SELECT DISTINCT sensor_id, ts::date AS day,
       first_value(value) OVER w AS first_value,
       last_value(value)  OVER w AS last_value
FROM readings
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY sensor_id, ts::date ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING);
exercises.explanation: With the default frame (`… AND CURRENT ROW`), `last_value()` returns the current row’s value, so even after `DISTINCT` you get well over a thousand rows instead of one per sensor and day. Extending the frame to `UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING` lets it see the whole day. Two `DISTINCT ON` queries joined together, or `array_agg(value ORDER BY ts)`, also work.

exercises.title: The next page, without OFFSET
exercises.task: The catalogue is listed in order of `(published, id)`, and the reader has scrolled as far as *Kindred* (`published` 1979, `id` 8). Return the next page: the five books that come right after it, with `id`, `title`, `published`, in that order.
exercises.hint: Compare rows: `(a, b) > (x, y)`.
exercises.solution:
SELECT id, title, published FROM books
WHERE (published, id) > (1979, 8)
ORDER BY published, id
LIMIT 5;
exercises.explanation: A row comparison orders like the sort key, so `(published, id) > (1979, 8)` means "after this row", and an index on `(published, id)` can jump straight there instead of reading and discarding `OFFSET` rows. `published > 1979` skips the other 1979 book; `published >= 1979 AND id > 8` drops every later book with a smaller id.

exercises.title: Loans per member per month
exercises.task: For members with at least one loan in the first half of 2025, return `name` and six columns `jan`, `feb`, `mar`, `apr`, `may`, `jun` counting their loans dated in each month of 2025 (0 when none).
exercises.solution:
SELECT m.name,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE extract(month FROM l.loaned_on) = 1) AS jan,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE extract(month FROM l.loaned_on) = 2) AS feb,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE extract(month FROM l.loaned_on) = 3) AS mar,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE extract(month FROM l.loaned_on) = 4) AS apr,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE extract(month FROM l.loaned_on) = 5) AS may,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE extract(month FROM l.loaned_on) = 6) AS jun
FROM members m JOIN loans l ON l.member_id = m.id
WHERE l.loaned_on >= '2025-01-01' AND l.loaned_on < '2025-07-01'
GROUP BY m.id, m.name;
exercises.explanation: `count(*) FILTER (WHERE …)` counts a subset of the group, so one pass produces all six columns, and an empty month is 0 rather than NULL (`sum(CASE … END)` without `ELSE 0` would give NULL). Restricting to 2025 matters: `extract(month …)` alone would also count Esther’s loan from June 2024.

exercises.title: Most borrowed book of each decade
exercises.task: Group books by publication decade (`published / 10 * 10`, e.g. 1960). For each decade, return `decade`, `title` and `loans` for the most-loaned book(s) of that decade, ties included. Only books loaned at least once take part.
exercises.explanation: Here integer division is what you want: `1968 / 10 * 10` is 1960. Aggregate first, then rank within each decade; `rank()` keeps ties (the 1980s have one), while `DISTINCT ON` or `row_number()` would arbitrarily keep only one.

exercises.title: Days between a member’s loans
exercises.task: For every loan return `member` (name), `loaned_on` and `days_since_prev`: days since the same member’s previous loan (an integer; NULL for their first).
exercises.explanation: `lag()` with `PARTITION BY member_id` looks at the previous loan of the same member only; without the partition it would compare with whoever borrowed just before. Date minus date is an integer, and minus NULL is NULL for the first loan.

exercises.title: Each customer’s most recent order
exercises.task: Return `customer`, `order_id` and `ordered_at` for the latest order of every customer who has ordered at least once. Customers with no orders are not listed.
exercises.hint: Try `DISTINCT ON`, a window function, or `LATERAL … LIMIT 1`.
exercises.solution:
SELECT DISTINCT ON (c.id) c.name AS customer, o.id AS order_id, o.ordered_at
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
ORDER BY c.id, o.ordered_at DESC;
exercises.explanation: `DISTINCT ON (c.id)` keeps the first row per customer in `ORDER BY` order, so ordering by `ordered_at DESC` within each customer picks the latest. The `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY …)` and `LATERAL (… LIMIT 1)` forms give the same rows. Taking `max(o.id)` assumes ids follow time; Ada’s order 103 is newer than her order 110.

exercises.title: Category breadcrumbs
exercises.task: Return `name` and `path` for every category, where `path` lists the names from the top-level category down, joined with `' > '` (e.g. `Electronics > Laptops`). Order by `path`.
exercises.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
  SELECT id, name, name AS path FROM categories WHERE parent_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, c.name, t.path || ' > ' || c.name
  FROM categories c JOIN tree t ON c.parent_id = t.id
)
SELECT name, path FROM tree ORDER BY path;
exercises.explanation: The anchor selects the roots; each recursive step attaches the children of rows found so far and extends their path. Unlike a fixed self-join, this works for any depth of tree.

exercises.title: Running revenue
exercises.task: For every non-cancelled order, in time order, return `order_id`, `ordered_at`, `total` (sum of its lines) and `running_total`: revenue of all non-cancelled orders up to and including this one.
exercises.solution:
SELECT o.id AS order_id, o.ordered_at, sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS total,
       sum(sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)) OVER (ORDER BY o.ordered_at) AS running_total
FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY o.id
ORDER BY o.ordered_at;
exercises.explanation: Window functions are evaluated after `GROUP BY`, so `sum(sum(…)) OVER (ORDER BY …)` runs a window sum over the per-order totals. With `ORDER BY` in the window, the default frame runs from the first row to the current one (and peers with the same timestamp, of which there are none here).

exercises.title: Order statuses per country
exercises.task: Return one row per customer country with `country` and four columns `pending`, `paid`, `shipped`, `cancelled`, each counting that country’s orders with that status (0 when none). Countries whose customers have no orders still appear, with zeros.
exercises.solution:
SELECT c.country,
       count(o.id) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'pending')   AS pending,
       count(o.id) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'paid')      AS paid,
       count(o.id) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'shipped')   AS shipped,
       count(o.id) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.country;
exercises.explanation: An aggregate with `FILTER (WHERE …)` only sees the rows that pass the filter, which turns the status values into columns in a single pass. `count` returns 0 for an empty set, whereas `sum(CASE WHEN … THEN 1 END)` returns NULL.

exercises.title: Best sellers per top-level category
exercises.task: Count units sold (sum of `quantity` over non-cancelled orders) per product. For each **top-level** category, return `category`, `product` and `units` for products ranked in the top 3 by units, **ties included** (a tie for third place returns both).
exercises.solution:
SELECT category, product, units FROM (
  SELECT top.name AS category, p.name AS product, sum(oi.quantity) AS units,
         rank() OVER (PARTITION BY top.id ORDER BY sum(oi.quantity) DESC) AS r
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id AND o.status <> 'cancelled'
  JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
  JOIN categories c ON c.id = p.category_id
  JOIN categories top ON top.id = COALESCE(c.parent_id, c.id)
  GROUP BY top.id, top.name, p.id, p.name
) t WHERE r <= 3;
exercises.explanation: Rank inside each top-level category after aggregating, then filter in an outer query (window results cannot be used in `WHERE`). ThinkPad and keyboard tie on 2 units for third place in Electronics; `rank()` keeps both, `row_number()` keeps an arbitrary one. Leaving the cancelled order in would lift the MacBook (3 units) into second place and push both of them out.

exercises.title: A daily 18:00 departure across a clock change
exercises.task: AA100 leaves New York every day at **18:00 local time**. For each day from 2025-03-07 to 2025-03-11, return `day` (a `date`) and `dep_utc`: that departure as a `timestamptz`. Order by `day`.
exercises.hint: Build the local wall-clock time first, then say which zone it belongs to.
exercises.explanation: A `timestamp` plus `AT TIME ZONE` means "this wall-clock time in that zone", so each day resolves with the offset in force that day: 23:00 UTC before 9 March, 22:00 UTC from 9 March on. Starting from one UTC instant and adding `interval '1 day'` in a UTC session keeps 23:00 every day and is wrong from the 9th on.

exercises.title: Apply seat requests
exercises.task: Apply every row of `seat_requests` to `bookings` in one statement: if the passenger has a **confirmed** booking on that flight, set its `seat`; otherwise insert a new confirmed `economy` booking with the requested `seat` and `fare` and `booked_at = '2025-03-01 00:00+00'`. The check lists `flight_id`, `passenger_id`, `seat`, `fare`, `status` of the affected flights.
exercises.hint: `MERGE INTO bookings b USING seat_requests r ON … WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE … WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT …`.
exercises.solution:
MERGE INTO bookings b
USING seat_requests r
   ON b.passenger_id = r.passenger_id AND b.flight_id = r.flight_id AND b.status = 'confirmed'
WHEN MATCHED THEN
  UPDATE SET seat = r.seat
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT (flight_id, passenger_id, class, fare, seat, status, booked_at)
  VALUES (r.flight_id, r.passenger_id, 'economy', r.fare, r.seat, 'confirmed', '2025-03-01 00:00+00');
exercises.explanation: `MERGE` decides per source row whether it matches a target row and runs the right branch, in one statement. Liam’s only booking on flight 16 is cancelled, so it must not match: leaving `b.status = 'confirmed'` out of the `ON` condition would give that cancelled booking a seat instead of creating a new one.
exercises.check: SELECT flight_id, passenger_id, seat, fare, status FROM bookings WHERE flight_id IN (9, 10, 16, 22);

exercises.title: Clear out cancelled flights and refund
exercises.task: Delete **every** booking on a cancelled flight. In the same statement, insert into `refunds` one row per deleted booking that was **confirmed**: `booking_id`, `passenger_id`, `amount` = its fare. The check returns `remaining` (bookings left) next to each refund row.
exercises.hint: `WITH gone AS (DELETE FROM bookings b USING flights f WHERE … RETURNING b.*) INSERT INTO refunds SELECT …`.
exercises.solution:
WITH gone AS (
  DELETE FROM bookings b USING flights f
  WHERE f.id = b.flight_id AND f.status = 'cancelled'
  RETURNING b.id, b.passenger_id, b.fare, b.status
)
INSERT INTO refunds (booking_id, passenger_id, amount)
SELECT id, passenger_id, fare FROM gone WHERE status = 'confirmed';
exercises.explanation: `DELETE … USING` joins the target to another table to decide which rows go, and `RETURNING` exposes the deleted rows to the outer `INSERT`, so nothing is lost between two statements. Liam’s already-cancelled booking is deleted but not refunded.
exercises.check: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM bookings) AS remaining, booking_id, passenger_id, amount FROM refunds;

exercises.title: Raise the lowest-paid engineers, with an audit trail
exercises.task: Give a 5% raise (rounded to a whole number) to every **Engineering** employee whose salary is below the Engineering average, and record each new salary in `salary_history` with `effective_from = '2026-01-01'`. Ideally in one statement. The check lists `id`, current `salary`, and the 2026 history salary for every employee.
exercises.hint: `WITH raised AS (UPDATE … RETURNING …) INSERT INTO salary_history SELECT … FROM raised`.
exercises.solution:
WITH raised AS (
  UPDATE employees e SET salary = round(e.salary * 1.05)
  WHERE e.dept_id = (SELECT id FROM departments WHERE name = 'Engineering')
    AND e.salary < (SELECT avg(salary) FROM employees WHERE dept_id = e.dept_id)
  RETURNING e.id, e.salary
)
INSERT INTO salary_history (emp_id, effective_from, salary)
SELECT id, '2026-01-01', salary FROM raised;
exercises.explanation: Every sub-statement of a `WITH` sees the same snapshot, so the average is computed from the salaries before the raise, and `RETURNING` hands the new values to the `INSERT`. Comparing against the company-wide average instead of the department’s picks the wrong people.

exercises.title: Share of six-figure earners
exercises.task: For each department that has employees, return `department` and `pct` = the percentage of its employees earning **more than 100000**, as a numeric rounded to 1 decimal (Sales: 50.0).
exercises.hint: What is `3 / 4` in PostgreSQL?
exercises.solution:
SELECT d.name AS department,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE e.salary > 100000) / count(*), 1) AS pct
FROM departments d JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.name;
exercises.explanation: `count()` returns bigint, and integer division truncates: `count(…) / count(*)` is 0 for every department below 100%, and `* 100` afterwards does not bring it back. Make one operand numeric *before* dividing (`100.0 * …`). `FILTER (WHERE …)` counts a subset inside the same group.

exercises.title: Departments as JSON documents
exercises.task: Return one row per department (all five) with `department` and `staff`: a JSON array of objects `{"name": …, "salary": …}` ordered by salary descending, then name. A department with nobody in it gets an empty array `[]`, not NULL.
exercises.hint: `json_agg(… ORDER BY …)` plus `COALESCE`.
exercises.solution:
SELECT d.name AS department,
       COALESCE(json_agg(json_build_object('name', e.name, 'salary', e.salary) ORDER BY e.salary DESC, e.name)
                FILTER (WHERE e.id IS NOT NULL), '[]') AS staff
FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.name;
exercises.explanation: With a `LEFT JOIN`, an empty department still produces one row of NULLs, and `json_agg` would turn it into `[{"name":null,"salary":null}]`. `FILTER (WHERE e.id IS NOT NULL)` makes the aggregate see no rows, which yields NULL, and `COALESCE(…, '[]')` turns that into an empty array.

exercises.title: Remove duplicates, then forbid them
exercises.task: Delete duplicate readings so that each `(sensor_id, ts)` appears once (the duplicates are exact copies), then add a **primary key** on `(sensor_id, ts)`. The check returns `total_rows`, `distinct_keys` and `pk_columns` (the primary key columns as text).
exercises.hint: Exact duplicates are told apart by their physical row id, `ctid`.
exercises.explanation: Two identical rows cannot be told apart by any column, but each has a distinct `ctid`; joining the table to itself and deleting the copy with the higher `ctid` keeps exactly one. The primary key would fail to build while duplicates exist, and afterwards it stops new ones arriving (an `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` then ignores repeats).

exercises.title: Fill a gap by linear interpolation
exercises.task: Sensor 3 missed the slots 2025-03-03 12:00 to 12:30 UTC. For each of those four slots return `slot` and `value`: the straight-line interpolation in time between the nearest reading before and the nearest reading after the slot, rounded to 2 decimals. Order by `slot`.
exercises.hint: One `LATERAL … ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 1` for the previous reading and one for the next.
exercises.solution:
SELECT g.slot,
       round(p.value + (n.value - p.value)
             * extract(epoch FROM g.slot - p.ts) / extract(epoch FROM n.ts - p.ts), 2) AS value
FROM generate_series(timestamptz '2025-03-03 12:00+00', timestamptz '2025-03-03 12:30+00', interval '10 minutes') AS g(slot)
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT ts, value FROM readings WHERE sensor_id = 3 AND ts < g.slot ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 1) p
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT ts, value FROM readings WHERE sensor_id = 3 AND ts > g.slot ORDER BY ts LIMIT 1) n
ORDER BY g.slot;
exercises.explanation: Each `LATERAL` subquery runs per generated slot and finds its nearest neighbour on one side through the index. The fraction of the way along is a ratio of epoch seconds; `extract(epoch …)` returns numeric, so no integer division sneaks in. Averaging the two neighbours gives the same value for every slot, which is not what was asked.

exercises.title: One open loan per member and book
exercises.task: Make it impossible for a member to have two **unreturned** loans of the same book, while still allowing any number of returned ones. The check reads the catalog: `is_unique`, `columns` (the indexed columns, sorted by name) and `predicate`.
exercises.hint: A unique index can have a `WHERE` clause.
exercises.solution: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX loans_one_open ON loans (member_id, book_id) WHERE returned_on IS NULL;
exercises.explanation: A partial unique index enforces uniqueness only among the rows that satisfy its predicate, here the open loans. A plain `UNIQUE (member_id, book_id)` constraint would also forbid borrowing a book again after returning it, and fails on this data anyway.
exercises.check:
SELECT i.indisunique AS is_unique,
       (SELECT string_agg(a.attname, ',' ORDER BY a.attname) FROM pg_attribute a WHERE a.attrelid = i.indrelid AND a.attnum = ANY (i.indkey)) AS columns,
       pg_get_expr(i.indpred, i.indrelid) AS predicate
FROM pg_index i WHERE i.indrelid = 'loans'::regclass AND NOT i.indisprimary;

exercises.title: Import members, duplicates and all
exercises.task: Load `member_import` into `members` keyed by `email`: new emails become new members with `joined = '2025-07-01'`; existing emails get their `name` and `tier` overwritten. The import lists one email **twice**: the row with the higher `import_id` wins. The check lists `email`, `name`, `tier`, `joined` of all members.
exercises.hint: Try a plain `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE` first and read the error.
exercises.solution:
INSERT INTO members (name, email, joined, tier)
SELECT DISTINCT ON (email) name, email, date '2025-07-01', tier
FROM member_import
ORDER BY email, import_id DESC
ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name, tier = EXCLUDED.tier;
exercises.explanation: `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` refuses to touch the same row twice in one statement ("command cannot affect row a second time"), so the input must be de-duplicated first; `DISTINCT ON (email) … ORDER BY email, import_id DESC` keeps the latest row per email. `EXCLUDED` is the row that was proposed for insertion, and existing members keep their original `joined`.
exercises.check: SELECT email, name, tier, joined FROM members;

exercises.title: Promote frequent borrowers
exercises.task: In one statement, set `tier = 'gold'` for every member with **at least 4 loans dated in 2025**. Do not touch anyone else. The check lists `id` and `tier` of all members, by id.
exercises.solution:
UPDATE members m SET tier = 'gold'
FROM (
  SELECT member_id FROM loans
  WHERE loaned_on >= '2025-01-01' AND loaned_on < '2026-01-01'
  GROUP BY member_id HAVING count(*) >= 4
) busy
WHERE busy.member_id = m.id;
exercises.explanation: `UPDATE … FROM` joins the target to another relation; aggregating in a subquery first gives at most one row per member, so each member is updated once. Esther has four loans in total but only three in 2025, and Dmitri has exactly four, so both the year filter and `>=` matter.
exercises.check: SELECT id, tier FROM members ORDER BY id;

exercises.title: Replace the nightly fines loop
exercises.task: The starter code computes fines one loan at a time. Do the same in a single `INSERT … SELECT`: a loan is late if it was returned after `due_on`, or is still out on 2025-06-30 and `due_on` is before that day. Fine = 0.25 per day late (up to the return date, or to 2025-06-30 if still out), capped at 10.00. The check lists `loan_id`, `amount` from `fines`.
exercises.solution:
INSERT INTO fines (loan_id, amount)
SELECT id, LEAST((COALESCE(returned_on, date '2025-06-30') - due_on) * 0.25, 10.00)
FROM loans
WHERE COALESCE(returned_on, date '2025-06-30') > due_on;
exercises.explanation: One set-based statement lets the planner scan the table once instead of running a separate `INSERT` per row from a procedural loop. `COALESCE` turns "still out" into "late until today", and `LEAST` applies the cap; forgetting the `COALESCE` silently drops every unreturned loan, because NULL minus a date is NULL.

exercises.title: Book in a delivery
exercises.task: A delivery arrived: 20 × product 7, 30 × product 8, and 10 × a new product 9, `Programming Rust` (category 5, price 59.90). In one statement, insert the new product and **add** the delivered quantity to the stock of existing ones. The check lists `id` and `stock` of all products.
exercises.hint: `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET stock = …`. Which row does `EXCLUDED` refer to?
exercises.solution:
INSERT INTO products (id, name, category_id, price, stock) VALUES
  (7, 'USB-C Hub', 6, 59.00, 20),
  (8, 'Mechanical Keyboard', 6, 129.00, 30),
  (9, 'Programming Rust', 5, 59.90, 10)
ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET stock = products.stock + EXCLUDED.stock;
exercises.explanation: In `DO UPDATE`, the table name refers to the existing row and `EXCLUDED` to the row you tried to insert. `SET stock = EXCLUDED.stock` overwrites the hub’s 100 units with 20 instead of adding them. The upsert is atomic, so no concurrent insert can slip in between a check and the write.
exercises.check: SELECT id, stock FROM products ORDER BY id;

exercises.title: Revenue with subtotals
exercises.task: Over non-cancelled orders, return `country`, `category` (top-level category name) and `revenue` (sum of `quantity * unit_price`) for every country–category pair, **plus** one subtotal row per country (category NULL) and one grand-total row (both NULL), all from one query.
exercises.solution:
SELECT cu.country, top.name AS category, sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
FROM order_items oi
JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id AND o.status <> 'cancelled'
JOIN customers cu ON cu.id = o.customer_id
JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
JOIN categories c ON c.id = p.category_id
JOIN categories top ON top.id = COALESCE(c.parent_id, c.id)
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((cu.country, top.name), (cu.country), ());
exercises.explanation: `GROUPING SETS` computes several groupings in one pass and fills the columns a set does not group by with NULL; here that is the same as `ROLLUP (cu.country, top.name)`. When the data itself can contain NULLs, `GROUPING(col)` tells a subtotal row from a real NULL group.

exercises.title: Restock everything that is sold out
exercises.task: In **one statement**, set `stock = 50` for every product whose stock is 0, and return the `id` and `name` of the products you changed. The check lists `id` and `stock` of all products afterwards.
exercises.hint: `UPDATE … RETURNING`.
exercises.solution: UPDATE products SET stock = 50 WHERE stock = 0 RETURNING id, name;
exercises.explanation: `RETURNING` sends back the modified rows, which saves a second round trip and avoids a race between "find" and "change". The checker compares the whole table afterwards.
exercises.check: SELECT id, stock FROM products ORDER BY id;
